rv.q: Lucy Kirkwood’s The Welkin is a mighty new play: magnificent in its scope, depth and intricacy. It’s a play that responds amply to the call for the National Theatre to stage more work by and about women by filling the stage with an ensemble of excellent female actors, led by Maxine Peake.
The Welkin is one of her most deliciously ambitious works to date, admirably large in scale.
This makes it arduous and even slightly sterile to watch at times but also profoundly admirable.
For all its quality, the evening left me tantalised and disturbed (and not in the way intended).
It is relentlessly interesting, but for me it's the dependence on melodramatic reveals to advance the plot that ultimately sinks 'The Welkin' a bit.
So why is The Welkin a bit of a slog?

It is currently staging a Nigerian Three Sisters, entertaining but marred by dauntingly chewy African accents. Now comes The Welkin, a new Lucy Kirkwood play set on the Norfolk-Suffolk border in 1759. The programme lists Michaela Kennen as dialect coach.
Kirkwood makes it hard for us to take much of an interest either way.
The Welkin makes for compelling viewing and is almost certain to be one of the best new plays this year.
Kirkwood's dramatic, highly articulate vision transcends both those influences. As she proved in the past, her voice is not only powerful but very much her own.
But it is a brilliant, brave, bold and intelligent three hours in the theatre.
But the play's glory lies in the short final sequences, which are beautiful and heartbreaking to watch.
I really wanted to love this show, but the muddy production makes that very hard labour.
